speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO SALE OF WINTER CATCH
speechtext:

This review is in progress, and until a report is forthcoming the hon. member will realize that I am not in a position to make any further statement.

speechtext: Will the Minister of Finance take the house into his confidence with respect to the McGinn case, which has been referred to before? It has to do with a wartime prices and trade board order. Will the minister inform the house whether an appeal has been or will be taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECISION OF ONTARIO SUPREME COURT IN MCGINN CASE
speechtext: The answer is that an appeal has not been taken. The judgment was a verbal judgment. The appeal related to the "just and reasonable" provisions in section 8 of the wartime prices and trade board order. A seller of nails was convicted of selling at prices that were higher than reasonable and just, having regard to the provisions of the order. He appealed on two or three grounds, including the ground that the evidence adduced did not justify the finding of the trial court. I am informed that the court of appeal maintained the appeal on that particular ground I am bringing to the attention of my colleagues the question whether an appeal should be taken, but my own personal view is that one should not be taken.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising to take part in this debate is to deal with certain matters affecting shipping and the shipbuilding industry; to refer at the same time to certain misconceptions which seem to be present in the minds of hon. members con-


cerning these industries; to deal with statements that have been made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), and, if time permits, to make reference to the statement made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) about the royal commission on transportation.
Prior to the war practically no deep-sea cargo ships were built in this country, and certainly none were being operated under the Canadian flag. We had a ship repairing industry but we had no shipbuilding industry. When I say that, I mean it in the sense that we had no shipbuilding industry engaged in the construction of deep-sea dry cargo vessels.
Twice in the last thirty-five years, as a part of our war effort, we have been called upon to build up these industries at considerable expense to the country. These industries, like many others in Canada, were the product of war necessity. The ships which we built were munitions of war. They were good ships, but they were built for a purpose, and they were built to a standard type in an emergency.
At the cessation of hostilities there were in Canada some 109 dry cargo vessels of the 10,000 ton type, and forty vessels of the 4,700 ton type. These vessels had been built in Canada. They were owned by the Canadian government and operated by the Canadian government under the Canadian flag. In addition to these 149 vessels there were 104 ships built in Canada which were lent to the United Kingdom under the mutual aid program, or chartered to the United Kingdom for operation under the United Kingdom flag to assist in the war effort of that country. That made a total of 253 ships. Twenty-six of the 104 ships have now been returned to Canada; fifty-eight more will be returned in 1950, and the balance of twenty is being retained by the United Kingdom. Of the ships owned by the government of Canada at the cessation of hostilities, eighteen were sold foreign, and twenty were retained by the United Kingdom under the mutual aid settlement. The remainder, including fifty-eight vessels yet to be returned by the British government, a total of 215 ships, were sold to Canadian operators with the proviso that they should not be transferred to foreign registry without the consent of the government.
The member for Vancouver South-and I am sorry he is not in his seat at the moment -accuses the government of lack of policy. I am delighted to see him coming into the chamber now. These ships were sold by the government to private Canadian operators, at reasonable prices, under a deliberate and

carefully-outlined policy of creating a merchant fleet under the Canadian flag.
For the first two years after the sale the operation was profitable and provided good wages for Canadian seamen. Furthermore, late in 1947 an independent body, the Canadian maritime commission, was created for the very purpose of advising the government from time to time on policies relating to the maintenance of the shipping and shipbuilding industries. Shortly after its creation the commission, at the beginning of 1948, foreseeing the time when competition for cargoes would be keen and would become keener as freights declined, advised the government to adopt a replacement plan. That time has now arrived. Freight rates have declined by about twenty per cent on a general average, and world shipping today has become overtonnaged.
Even during the war years, foreign nations were planning on replacing the tonnage destroyed. Nearly three years ago they initiated a construction program which was limited only by the capacity of their yards and their ability to secure or produce steel. In the two-year period from December 31, 1946, to December 31, 1948, the United Kingdom and other traditional maritime nations added over ten million deadweight tons to their dry cargo merchant fleets. It is evident that the introduction of such a volume of tonnage, including many newer and speedier ships, must put the Canadian wartime-built fleets at a decided disadvantage in competing for available cargoes.
The statistical position is that in spite of a contracting international trade, world shipping tonnage seeking employment is now about thirty per cent greater than it was prior to the war. Up until recently the increased tonnage of the United Kingdom and other foreign nations has been absorbed into international shipping at the expense of the United States. It must be obvious that all of Canada's 215 war-built vessels cannot hope to compete under these conditions, and that owners in liner trades particularly must replace their vessels with faster and more modern craft in order to compete with foreign vessels. The government is willing to help these operators to do this, but the desire and the incentive to remain in the shipping business depend upon the operators themselves. I submit that the wisdom of the replacement plan, which is one of the means devised to assist operators in obtaining new and modern tonnage, is fully justified.
I should like to say a word in explanation of the replacement plan. If an owner, feeling the need to improve his competitive posi-29087-70
The Address-Mr. Chevrier tion, desires to sell a ship which he has purchased under the restrictive flag covenant, he applies to the commission for permission to do so. The commission considers all aspects of the application, including the effect of the proposed sale on Canadian trade and employment. If the commission is satisfied that the sale is in the interests of the country as a whole, it recommends to the government that permission be granted. As a condition to the sale, however, the owner must place the whole of the purchase money in escrow. If the owner still owes money to the crown on the original purchase of the ship, the commission permits him to borrow out of the escrow funds sufficient money to enable him to pay off his mortgage, but the loan must be replaced. In effect the plan creates a compulsory building reserve to secure replacement within five years from the date of sale, with a possible two-year extension.
Under the plan thus far, twenty-six vessels have been sold, twenty-one 10,000 tonners and five 4,700 tonners. These sales have been approved for transfer out of Canadian flag. The gross proceeds of the sales, amounting to $16,602,250, are being paid to escrow. The policy in this plan is to provide the Canadian merchant marine with modern fast vessels which will be able to meet foreign flag competition.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In deciding whether owners may sell vessels abroad, due regard is had as to whether the ships can obtain profitable employment under the Canadian flag, and whether the sale would have detrimental effects upon Canada's trade. In some cases permission to sell has been refused. The replacement will proceed on a gradual and orderly basis and is not a wholesale slashing of the Canadian fleet, as some would like us to believe. Surely it is better, instead of having a ship laid up-when it rapidly deteriorates, and gives no employment to Canadian crews-to allow it to be sold and the proceeds used to secure a better ship built by Canadian labour.
This brings me to the question of how large a Canadian-flag fleet we can reasonably expect to support in this country. After the war Canada operated the fifth largest fleet in the world. As our war-built fleet did not appear on the high seas until about 1943, we

were fortunate enough to escape the heavy losses suffered by the United Kingdom and our other allies. We therefore jumped from having practically no fleet at all to the position of being a major maritime power. The United States likewise built a tremendous fleet for war purposes the like of which had not been seen before. Since the war the United Kingdom, Norway, Denmark, Holland, Sweden and other countries have been rapidly replacing their war losses, since their very existence depends upon their fleets. Not only these but other countries such as South Africa, Australia, Argentina and India, who were not substantially engaged in seafaring, are now embarking upon a maritime program. The result is that at this immediate moment, as I have stated before, the world is over-tonnaged.
It has been suggested that Canada should adopt restrictive practices, such as attaching conditions to her export trade. The hon. member for Vancouver South suggested that fifty per cent of our exports should be carried in Canadian bottoms. I wonder how much thought he has given to that suggestion.
I wonder if he knows the difficulties and complications which have attended a similar restriction as it was put into effect in the United States. Under the conditions I have outlined, the policy as it is in operation now in the United States is hurting the trade of that country. The United States is giving away vast sums of money for the rehabilitation of Europe; and in its wisdom congress has laid down that part of the money so given must be spent in American shipping services. You may ask why Canada does not do the same thing. Canada is still straining her economy to the utmost to restore the buying power of her customers abroad. If, however, we say to the foreign buyer, "You must ship in Canadian bottoms, using scarce dollars," he will go elsewhere; and this at a time when we are anxious to sell our surplus Canadian goods. Such a policy would drive away trade rather than encourage it.
It is startling to find the hon. member for Vancouver South making this suggestion. The United Kingdom must find means of paying for our grain and timber. One such means is by way of her shipping services; but if we were to follow the hon. member's suggestion that fifty per cent of our exports to the United Kingdom must be carried in Canadian-flag bottoms it would mean that our farmers and our producers generally would have still greater difficulty in disposing of their products. It would mean that the lumberman in British Columbia would have the same difficulty in disposing of his goods.
The Address-Mr. Chevrier The suggestion of the hon. member involves further restrictions on British buying power in Canada. Our Canadian shipping must be the tool of trade, rather than a means of preventing trade. It is all very well for members of the opposition, who have no responsibility, to make these suggestions. As far as I am concerned I have no intention of being a party to any scheme which would prejudice the interests of Canadian producers, and of the country as a whole, in order to benefit any one group.
Another suggestion made by the hon. member is that it may be necessary "to have some provision for government subsidies." Again I wonder how much time he has spent in research on this subject. Having regard to the size of the Canadian fleet at the present time, and having regard to the number of ships that will be returned to Canada in 1950, does the hon. gentleman have any idea what it would cost per annum to subsidize a fleet on that basis? It would cost the Canadian people at least $20 million a year to put our ships on a competitive basis with other British ships, and still provide no guarantee that they would be employed.

Hon. members must realize that deep-sea shipping is an international market, at present severely restricted by the exchange difficulties of other nations. Canadian ships must earn dollars to pay then-wages. The suggestion that fifty per cent of Canadian exports should be carried in Canadian ships is obviously completely unrealistic in the light of today's world trading conditions. Do not think for one minute the government is not actively concerned in seeing that the Canadian fleet is employed. Had it not been for the activities of the Canadian maritime commission last year, I think it can safely be said that a number of Canadian ships would be laid up and lying idle on account of inability to procure cargoes.
I am glad to say that at the moment no Canadian ship is permanently laid up for lack of employment. The policy of the government is that a reasonable proportion of cargoes purchased in Canada should be carried in Canadian-flag bottoms. What that reasonable proportion is, must of necessity depend upon a number of circumstances, and particularly upon the circumstances of the trade. The Canadian maritime commission is in constant negotiation with shippers and buyers on this subject. As I said before, no Canadian ship is idle at the present time, but Canadian owners must realize it is up to them to modernize their fleets. The government is prepared to assist them, but they must first show their determination to help themselves and thus help the country maintain a Canadian-flag fleet.
It is likewise up to those employed on our Canadian ships to see that Canadian ships are operated with the same skill and efficiency as the ships of other flags. I regret that in the last few years a number of minor disputes and stoppages of work have impaired the efficiency of the Canadian-flag ships,

especially those engaged in liner service. If the differences between owners and labour cannot be resolved, the outlook for the future of Canadian shipping is not good.
From what I have said so far, it will be seen that there are so many factors involved that it is impossible to give an accurate estimate of the future size of the Canadian-flag fleet. It must depend upon the pattern of world trade and the ingenuity of the Canadian operator. Whatever the future may hold, the scheme of replacement as propounded by the Canadian maritime commission is a wise and constructive plan in its long-term implications. If some seamen are forced to seek other employment by reason of the operation of the plan, that is surely preferable to a situation under which the whole fleet grows gradually obsolete and can give no employment.
Let me say a word about the Canadian coastal trade. The member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said that Canadian shipowners were selling their ships either to Great Britain or to Greece; that Canadian seamen were being beached, and that these ships were not only taking our overseas trade from us but also were operating from port to port along the Canadian coast, thereby depriving us of our coastal trade. That statement is incorrect. There is not one Canadian vessel sold foreign with government approval under the replacement plan which has been or is now operating in the Canadian coastal trade. There has been no change in our coastal laws.
In the Canada Shipping Act we find the term "British ship registered in Canada", which of course means a vessel flying the Canadian flag, a Canadian ship. Such a vessel also falls within the ambit of the expression "British ship" as used in the act, which means a vessel owned and registered in any part of the commonwealth.
A ship which is not a British ship may not transport goods or passengers from one place in Canada to another place in Canada, either directly or by way of a foreign port. Furthermore, under part 13 of the act no foreign-built British ship-that is to say, a ship registered within the commonwealth but built outside the commonwealth-is entitled to engage in the Canadian coastal trade unless she pays a duty of twenty-five per cent of her value and is thereupon licensed to engage in coastal trade. Subject to this, every ship which engages in coastal trade must be built, registered and owned in some part of the commonwealth.
The act does give the governor in council the power to suspend those provisions, but this is only done in case of emergency, in an

isolated case where no British ship is available to carry the cargo. In practice what happens is that an application to use a nonBritish built ship is made to the customs and excise division of the Department of National Revenue. The application is referred to the Canadian maritime commission, which investigates the circumstances of the application and only recommends that permission be granted if it is urgent that the goods be carried, and if there is no Canadian or British ship available. When permission is granted to a non-British built ship, it is assessed and pays a proportionate share of the twenty-five per cent import duty, depending on the length of time of the particular voyage or voyages. An exception is made where the movement of grain from the head of the lakes to the bay ports is urgent and sufficient Canadian lake ships are not available. Then the Canadian wheat board is permitted to charter United States bottoms. The same situation exists in connection with the transportation of petroleum cargoes on the lakes, but the twenty-five per cent is still paid. Apart from the lake trade, in all the innumerable coastal voyages which took place in Canada during 1948, there were only eighteen cases in which such recommendations were made, and then only because it was in the interests of the country that the goods be moved and no suitable Canadian or British bottoms were available at the time.
These provisions were inserted in the act for the purpose of restricting the coastal trade in Canada to vessels built and ewned in the commonwealth. The member for Cape Breton South, in his mistaken effort to prove that Canada was sacrificing her coastal trade to vessels of foreign flag, stated that Great Britain prohibited foreign vessels from engaging in her coastal trade, and recommended that we follow her example. He is again mistaken. There is no statutory provision in the United Kingdom which debars foreign shipping from participation in the United Kingdom coastal trade. This trade is open to the flags of all nations. There is, in fact, ,a considerable amount of foreign tonnage engaged in the United Kingdom coastal trade, and it will probably continue to be so engaged. Thus we see how confusing and misleading are the statements made by the members of the opposition on this subject.
Members of the opposition are undoubtedly trying to create the impression, for their own purposes, that the government is careless of the interests of shipowners and Canadian seagoing labour. Nothing could be further from the facts. To any reasonable person who knows the true situation, it is obvious that the government is doing everything in its power to maintain the industry on a sound
The Address-Mr. Chevrier basis and to give permanent employment to Canadian seamen.

If you go north from the main corner you run into the Prevost, which is the navy training station. Now is the time for the dominion government to get out of some of these spots and let

business take its regular course. It may be thought that I am placing a lot of emphasis upon this, but the facts are that there are 1,329 employees of the dominion government with a pay roll of $2,858,000 per year and a rentals and upkeep cost of $98,000 a year. -the accommodation at present occupied by both the navy and army in London is not satisfactory, but it will have to be retained until alternative accommodation can be secured. The reason I bring up this matter again is that in his speech the minister of health did not forecast the introduction of a blind-persons act. As perhaps all hon. members know, the Canadian council of the blind are sponsoring a six-point plan.
As their first point they ask that there should be a blind-persons act rather than the Old Age Pensions Act. They feel that their
The Address-Mr. Manross problems are entirely different and I agree with them. They are not old age pensioners. As point No. two they ask that the word "pension" be discarded as far as the blind are concerned. They would like to have it called a blindness allowance. It is not a pension, it is not insurance against old age, it is simply a foundation for future enterprise.
No. three in their six-point program is the elimination of the means test. There should be no means test as far as the blind are concerned.
No. four is the request for an adequate blindness allowance in relation to the cost of living. We all know what that means under present circumstances. These people cannot get along on the regular pension rates. They are asking for an increase and I think they should have it. Between the ages of 20 and 40 years many of these people are learning Braille and craftwork and it is necessary that they have an allowance so that they may be able to live the kind of independent life lived by the normal citizen.
As No. five, they ask for a reduction of the residence requirement. Under the present regulations they must have lived in this country twenty years before qualifying for an allowance. Hon. members can understand how someone might be here only five years-we are after immigrants-and he might have an accident or something might happen to his eyes. They feel that as long as a person is a Canadian citizen he should be entitled to the allowance, whether he has been here one year or twenty years.
Their sixth point, which has to do with medical or surgical treatment for blind conditions, has been pretty well conceded. Most municipalities and provincial governments are assisting in this work.
The blind are a happy people; they are fine people to get along with. They do not want sympathy; they want to be independent. But they do feel that they should have a special blind-persons act, and I agree with them. I do not know how many hon. members have seen the Canadian council of the blind magazine Outlook, which is edited by the president of the council, who lives at 174 Devonshire street in my riding. She edits this magazine in an office in her home and is one of the two blind editors in Canada. She is doing a fine job.

At home we have been blessed with good crops.

That is quite fine. It is too bad that we were not blessed with a good government to sell those crops. However, that was left out. If we had had a government that had so arranged that those crops could have been sold at the right prices to increase the national income, so that the farmer got his proper share of that income, we would have been much better off, instead of having to cut down trees and throw away potatoes.
I was rather amused at the speech made the other day by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who had just come back from England. I was reminded of an apple dumpling-a lot of apples surrounded by crust. The minister had crust enough to try to make the Canadian farmers believe that England grows all the apples she needs, that she does not have to import any. Of course it has since been proved by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Stephenson) that the minister was wrong.
Then I would term the parliamentary assistant to the minister the whipped cream on the apple dumpling. He came up to London and Middlesex West and said that England was a land of milk and honey, that the people there had everything, that they were the best dressed and best fed people he had ever seen. The picture he painted was that the country was in great shape. Was that not a foul ball to pitch to the women's council or the women's club when they were engaged in collecting food parcels to ship to England? It took the wind out of their sails because they thought they were sending something that was needed. Of course, he thought that his statement would get out into the back concessions, and serve more or less as an alibi for the failure to sell our apples, potatoes and farm products. He thought that, if he could make them believe that England had everything, that would be a perfect reason why we could not sell anything. But they did not accept it. He should have gone over to his neighbour in the next farm, talked it over in the barnyard, and then left it there. Of course, you cannot expect a professional politician-I have not reached that stage yet-to make his bed and lie in it. Most of them make up their bunk and lie out of it.
The next paragraph of the speech from the throne has to do with the report of the royal commission on prices. I do not know whether I can talk about that under the rules, but there were many meetings of the prices committee before these royal birds were appointed with their big salaries. There was one fellow receiving $125 a day, which is not peanuts. We had hearings on bread, milk, butter and 
all those things, and the cost of living kept going up all the time because more taxes were required from the people to operate the committee. There are interruptions, Mr. Speaker. It is a great thing to have a lot of assistants. There is one thing I wish you would arrange, Mr. Speaker. I have a lot of parliamentary assistants but they do not get paid. If you will give them $1,000 apiece I am sure we will go great guns.
There is a provision in the speech from the throne for governmental assistance to the producers of iron and steel. What does that mean? It means that we have to assist the industry. But what is the purpose of the industrial development bank? Do they not, by lending money, attempt to fill the gap between the regular bank and the stock promoter? Oh, no; they will not do that because they want the situation handled in such a way that they can nationalize the steel industry. They want complete control over it.
There is a section of the speech from the throne which reads:
You will be asked to make the customary provision tor essential services. Prosperous conditions now prevailing are being reflected in the buoyant level of national revenues; a condition to which due consideration is being given by my ministers in the preparation of forthcoming budgetary proposals.
I do not know what that means. The optimists say it means that taxes are coming off, and the fellows who are not optimists, who think they know the top sources of authority in the government, say that they are going to keep the taxes on. Having been in the soft-drink business, I should perhaps make a special plea in that connection and ask the government to take the taxes off soft drinks and chocolate bars for the benefit of children. You cannot say that is selfish interest on my part, because I was in the business. Now the bank is; but the trouble is, it is not the industrial development bank.
Then there is another paragraph of the speech from the throne which says something about communists, and warns us about them. There is something that is really up to date. Our leader was talking about communists in 1938 and 1939, and everybody said that what he was saying was far-fetched and that he had a lot of funny ideas. Having known him for a number of years, however, I can say that he is not quite as funny as some people think. He usually thinks ahead pretty well. He projects his mind into the future. Of course I know that there is no one in the house who wants to increase the communist element in Canada. In my estimation the best way you can overcome it is by improving our own way of life. The more we can produce, the more we can have in our democratic way of life, the more envious the communists

will be, and the more they will think that democracy is a pretty good ticket. It is a strange thing, but you never see a happy communist. I do not know why that is, but you never see one. I suppose the reason is that communism is a sour ism based on envy and hatred of successful people. If the communists would spend less time hating and more time loving and pushing, as genuine Canadians do, they would not have any cause for envy. They would be happy then, but they would not be communists. Everybody is worried about communism, and we have to do what we can.
The people of your ridings and the people of my riding are worried about many things. No. 1 is the cost of living.

You are finished, because you would have to have an accountant and a lawyer to understand this form, and no two lawyers can agree on one thing.
Here are some of the items on which they have to supply information: crops and seeds, wheat, oats, barley, hay. It does not say whether it is tons of hay or hayseeds. There are an awful lot of hayseeds in London. Then there is an item for livestock, cattle, hogs, horses, sheep. You have to give information as to how many little piggie wiggies you had last year, how many of them died, and how many were sold. Then you come to the part dealing with mama. You have to show how much she used on the table last year. You have to show the value of the stuff you ate. How can you figure what the value is? Wheat is $1.55 and then you may get 20 cents more, and then 20 cents more. Pigs are so much one time and a different price another time. How are you going to know what she ate? Talk about controls; boy, the farmers are really under them. The next heading is "Livestock held for sale." For now, or the future value? Say I have two pigs and two calves; what are they going to be worth next year? You have to put that down or one of these 250 spies will be banging on your door. Then they wiill charge you not only what you did not pay -wi your income tax, but interest on what you should have thought you should pay. It is n great thing, this control.
Then we come to "Income tax not paid; how much?" You do not know when you make it out, but you have to answer that question. Can you imagine anyone putting that in? Living in the city, I do not have to put it in; that is done for me, but that is just another example of the magnitude of these powers under which they are trying to control the lives of all of us. A farmer does not only get this form, which is a complicated thing. He also gets this big book, twenty-seven pages long; and the last paragraph is headed, "If a farmer dies during the taxation year, who files the income tax return?" You may as well say, "If I should die before I wake, who my income tax will take?" And we pay for that; the taxpayers pay for it. That is something else wrapped up in all these emergency powers and controls. I do not wonder that the farmers are crabbing. I always thought they were the luckiest people in the world, though I know some now

The Address-Mr. Manross who are down to two cars. They are controlled just like us in the cities, so we need not think we are being picked on. We are all picked on under this system, and we want to get out of it. We are through with it.

I hope I am not trespassing on the ground of the hon. member who is going to follow me if I say a word about old age pensions, because I know that is one of his pet hobbies. However, I will not go very far with it. He asks what is the government's attitude in regard to old age pensions. Why, they made that clear last session in a bill they introduced. Here it is. A diplomat works for five

years and gets a pension of $3,000 a year. If he works ten years he gets $5,000 a year. That is their pension plan. And who gets the jobs? Henchmen. That is their policy in regard to old age pensions. They do not pay any attention to anyone else, because the old age pensioners do not go out and do anything for their party. They should think a little more about the deserving citizens of this country, the crippled, the invalids, the old and the blind. As you know, my pet hobby is the blind. I have worked with them and had the pleasure of being with them for a long time. It seems to me that this sort of thing is wrong, saying to certain diplomats, "You have been a good boy, Mr. So-and-So. You have done a lot of good for the party. We cannot send you to the Senate, but we will send you to Trinidad or Shangri-La and in five years you will be eligible for $3,000 a year for the rest of your life". That is a nice job. They buy tickets and charge them up, and we do not even see them on the boat. To me that is a kind of monkey business and monkey business is for monkeys. We should not indulge in that sort of thing; it is not good enough for Canadians, who are sick and tired of being pushed around.
I have not much more to say; I know hon. members will be glad of that. There has been a lot of double talk so far, and I hope the government will become more definite in their policies. They should have been more definite in the speech from the throne, because after all they write it and somebody else reads it. But they do not want to tell you what they are going to do. They will tell us before the election, no doubt; they will tell us a lot of things they are going to do, but if they get in they will never do them. But if they do not get back to their original role of being small "1" liberals they will not even form the official opposition. Some of the answers they give you remind me of something I saw in a Toronto paper the other evening. A chap was in talking to his banker, asking for a loan. The banker replied, "Well, Mr. Graham Towers is head of the industrial development bank, which is part of the Bank of Canada", and so on, and the fellow got pretty disappointed in the end. Finally he said, "Mr. Banker, does Graham Towers know more than God?" The banker replied, "I think so, but I doubt it". That is the sum and substance of some of the ministers' statements. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker was perfectly correct in his guess as to the subject on which I would speak in this debate, namely the right to old age security.

Since the end of last session I have been able to collect a considerable amount of new material on this subject though, as all hon. members are aware, the subject itself is not a new one for the representative in this chamber from Winnipeg North Centre. I mention the name of my riding to remind older members of this house that for a good many years my predecessor, the late Mr. Woodsworth, pressed the claims of older Canadians and fought for and won the beginnings of an old age pension system. Since coming to this house as his successor I have felt that this is indeed one of our most important domestic problems.
At the outset, I want to join with the large number of members on all sides of the house who have asked for some immediate relief for our present old age pensioners. The amount of pension varies from province to province across this country. In some provinces, it is only the $30 provided by the federal statute. I regret to have to say that is still the case in my own province of Manitoba. In other provinces provincial supplements are being paid. Even so, in no case can it be said that Canada's elder citizens are being properly treated. I sincerely hope that the government may see fit before this session ends to introduce legislation increasing the amount of the pension to at least $50 a month and bringing the eligible age down to sixty-five.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, it is my purpose to go a little bit further into this question of old age security and to argue once again, as strongly as I can, the case for putting old age pensions, indeed all forms of social security, on a firm foundation. This would mean moving in the direction of two things: on the one hand, an over-all social security scheme and, on the other hand, a contributory plan to make it possible to pay adequate benefits. As I proceed I shall have something to say about the details of what is involved in a contributory plan, but at the moment I simply outline that as the theme of my remarks this afternoon.
Without delay we should get our old age security, and our social security generally, on a much firmer foundation so that, on the one hand, people will receive proper benefits and, on the other hand, those benefits will go to all our people as a matter of right. We simply must get away from this degrading means test which is so unfair and so hard on so many of our people.
In connection with the demand for proper old age security, I would point out that labour is asking for it today in even stronger terms than ever before. Indeed, labour is respon-
The Address-Mr. Knowles sible for the emergence of the idea of an old age pension in this country. At the present time, many unions that are renegotiating collective agreements are concentrating on pension and retirement plans. In addition to the demands of labour on the employer on the one hand, and on the government on the other hand, for retirement plans, we have the counterpart of boards of trade and chambers of commerce passing resolutions, urging this government to get on with the business of setting up a proper old age pension and social security plan. In addition to what is being said by these bodies, industry, through its various publications, is claiming it is moving in that direction. Whatever industry's motive may be does not concern me at this moment. I am pointing out the fact that the idea of retirement or pension benefits for all the citizens of this country is becoming an accepted idea in all quarters.	.
Not only is it accepted by those groups to which I have referred, but some form of overall social security is now in the platforms of all political parties. I shall not take the time to indicate when those ideas got into the various platforms. I should say to the government, though, that the idea of old age pensions has been in the Liberal platform since 1919, which makes it shameful that they have done so little to put old age security on a proper basis in all those years.
I would say, also, that the experience of our older citizens at the present time, in their efforts to keep alive on the meagre amounts allotted to them, makes this question a vital one to us. All of us are human enough to be concerned for those who are now our elder brothers or sisters, and the amounts they receive simply do not sustain life properly at all. We all realize too, that sooner or later this problem is one we all must face.
I should like to suggest one other reason, Mr. Speaker, for the urgency of this problem, and that is the world situation. We are all conscious of the fact that we are in a world which is being subjected to a conflict of ideas. Basically, that is what is happening between the east and west. We who feel our idea is the superior one, who want our democratic idea to prevail, must face the fact that, if it is going to prevail, our people must become more thoroughly convinced that it is the correct one. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that so long as that freedom about which we are talking contains so much insecurity, our people are not thoroughly convinced that ours is really the better way, and that is the most serious weakness with which we are faced in this conflict of ideas. I suggest that nothing

The Address-Mr. Knowles could contribute more to our determination that our democratic way of life shall prevail than the building of security into the fabric of our life. I propose that the place to begin is with an old age security program as part of an over-all social security plan.
Last year, during the debate on the address I spoke on this same subject. That was on March 2, 1948. On that occasion I gave figures, which I obtained from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and which indicated that the problem of old age security is increasing as the years pass by. Some hon. members may remember that the house gave me permission to put on the record quite a few tables which I felt were useful to anyone studying this question. I am not going to repeat those figures, as there were too many of them. But I should like to refer to one set of figures which I gave the house at that time. These figures came from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and they indicate that in 1941 there were in Canada 767,815 people of 65 years of age and over. This represented 6-7 per cent of the total population of Canada in that year. According to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics forecast for the future, in 1971 the people of 65 years of age and over in Canada will be twice that number, namely, 1,523,000. This will represent 10-4 per cent of the anticipated Canadian population in 1971. It so happens that, in the same period in which there is this tremendous increase in the percentage of older people, there will also be a decrease in the percentage of children. On the other hand the group in between, namely the working population, will increase both in numbers and in percentage, according to this official forecast.
As I pointed out last year this means that, although the problem of old age security will be greater because of the larger number and the larger percentage of older people, it is also the case that there will be a larger group in the working brackets. This means the working group can produce extra wealth to make possible an adequate retirement for our older people. I pointed out last year, and I think it is worth repeating this year, that the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, which looks at these things objectively, made a most interesting comment. I quote from Bulletin No. F-4 put out by the bureau:
This trend-
That is, the increase in the number of older people.
-together with the increase of productive workers, suggests that the burden of dependency will be spread over a greater number of people, and hence the effect of an increase in the aged population with the heavier burden which it entails will not be so costly a problem per capita.

There is one other paragraph from the comment on this matter by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics that I should like to quote:
The trend toward an increasing proportion of old people in the population implies an intensification of the problems of the aged. The emphasis upon change and the depreciation of tradition prevalent in modern industrial society, and the social structure which such a society engenders have placed the aged in a precarious economic and social position in which more of the responsibility for their welfare is being of necessity assumed by the state.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we should keep ourselves conscious of this problem that is ahead of us in the next few decades. On the one hand, the number of our older people will increase, and we must be concerned with their welfare and their right to security. On the other hand, it is not an insoluble problem because our working force will increase, and we can produce more wealth. Therefore a larger proportion of current wealth can be used to provide a proper old age pension. It behooves us to consider what is being done today in a country like the United Kingdom. We are all conscious of the lack of resources and of the difficulties that country is facing. Despite those difficulties, if that country is doing what it is in terms of social security for all the people, from the cradle to the grave, surely we, with our much greater resources and with our expanding working force, should do not less -as is now the situation-but a great deal better.
In the face of this growing problem, as I thought about it and studied it between sessions, I asked this question: What are we doing? What are the statistics-indeed are there any-that would show whether or not we are making any headway in the matter of providing old age security? As I was pondering that question last summer, there came to me in the mail a copy of Industry, published by the Canadian Manufacturers Association. I found it to be a most interesting document. I look at it every time it comes, and I shall be quoting from other copies of it in other debates this session, for I must take issue with some of its statements. But this one which was issued in July, 1948, had on the front page an interesting article entitled "Without fanfare." The first paragraph reads as follows:
Many things socialism is promising labour are already in existence because capitalism has extended to thousands a great many employee benefits without any brassy publicity or fanfare of political trumpets.
As I read through the article I found that it gave figures indicating what private industry is doing in the matter of employee retire-

ment plans, health benefit plans and so on. Let me say that it is quite an impressive story. But having read that story, I wondered what the total picture might be; so I took the liberty of writing to the research division of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and set out a number of questions. At this moment I wish to express my thanks to the employees in that research division for the work they did. Considerable effort was involved on their part, and as a result of it, and of the references they gave me to other departments, I was able to put together a table that shows what we are doing in terms of providing for our own old age. As I say, I have this information in the form of a table which I should like to read to the house; I am not asking that it be put on Hansard without my reading it. But I hope that Hansard will be willing to put it in tabular form. As to provincial employees, I must point out that Quebec is not included. Those who did this work for me were unable to get figures with regard to Quebec. I would also point out that these figures do not include school teachers and other employees of school boards across the country. Solely on my own, I am suggesting figures so that we may try to build this picture up as nearly as possible to what it actually is. For example, since there are in Ontario 8,000 provincial employees contributing to pension plans, I suggest that it might be fair to take that figure for Quebec. It is just a guess, but I am sure that there are no more than that.
With regard to school board employees, including teachers and others, I suggest that we add roughly the same figure as would represent those who are contributing to municipal plans. I know in my own city of Winnipeg, for example, the school board budget is just about half the total city budget. This would seem to suggest that the number of employees is about equal as between school board and other municipal departments. Please note that I am not going into the question as to how many of these plans to which people are contributing are adequate. My fear is that many of them will prove to be inadequate. However, I have no way of finding out what the amounts are. I point out however that at the present time we have a large number of superannuated civil servants who are drawing retirement benefits which are now hopelessly inadequate, but to which they contributed in the years gone by.
In response to a question of mine figures were placed on Hansard a few days ago showing that 1,031 superannuated civil servants or widows are drawing pensions today of less than $20 a month; and, in fact, that a total of 3,743 superannuated civil servants or their widows, federal in all cases, are drawing pensions of less than $40 a month. That is the problem facing us now, and which will face us in the future-that with all the work being done by private industry and by superannuation and retirement plans of one kind or another, and with all the acceptance there is behind the idea that this sort of thing should be done, only 12J or 13 per cent of the number of people between twenty and sixty in the working brackets are now providing for their own old age.

To get back to my figures, this means that instead of 41 per cent of our elderly citizens receiving old age pensions, as obtains today, in the event of there being no change in the meantime we would have from 70 to 75 per cent of our elderly people in 1971 having to go on the old age pension.
Of necessity many of these figures are estimates; but they are estimates prepared by people who are in the business, and they cannot be very far out. and in this speech I am not detracting one iota from what is being done by way of making provision for old age by any agency whatsoever.
Surely this makes it evident the time has come to put our provision for old age security on a firm foundation. The only way it can be done is by an over-all contributory plan which calls for one contribution from the people of this country, in return for which there will be coverage for all the things which hit individual citizens from the cradle to the grave.
In addition to the argument which I have advanced already, that there are so few who are able to make provision for their old age, I would say that the other side of the argument holds true as well. We have reached the point where 15 per cent of our people are able to make provision for their old age, but it should be noted that many of those people are contributing to plans into which contributions are made by industry, and by the state or from the consolidated revenue fund. That means that many people are helping to provide pensions for others when they themselves are not able to qualify for a retirement plan. The only answer is an over-all scheme that includes everybody.
The Address-Mr. Knowles There is another aspect of the problem which is becoming quite acute. I refer to the man over forty years of age who finds trouble today getting employment. One reason, among many, that makes it difficult for such a man to get employment is that in many industries retirement plans are in operation. Employers are ready to admit that in many cases the man over forty may have more ability than a younger man, but they contend that if they employ the older man it ups the cost of their pension plans. The result is that a plan which is essentially good becomes a barrier to employment. The only answer again is an over-all plan that will take in everyone.
In connection with the need for over-all coverage I would cite the experience we have had in connection with a good piece of legislation now in existence, namely, unemployment insurance. I speak as a protagonist of that kind of legislation, but I would point out one serious difficulty that has been encountered. No matter how much you explain to a man who is out of work because of ill health that actuarially he is not covered, it still does not go down. You can tell him that unemployment insurance is like fire insurance in that you are lucky if you carry it for a number of years and do not have to draw on it. But, if a man has paid premiums for a number of years and becomes unemployed because of poor health and is unable to draw benefits, such explanations do not go down. I know because I have tried to give that explanation of the act as it now stands. The only answer to that is what I am proposing, that we move on from the kind of social security we now have in unemployment insurance to a wider scheme that provides protection against unemployment, ill health and old age, all in one piece of legislation.
I stated earlier that I intended to say something about the meaning of the word "contributory" in relation to social security. There are some who think of contributory social insurance only in terms of private life insurance set-ups which provide for the contributor getting back only the amount that he has paid in, plus such interest as that money may have earned. That creates all sorts of problems when you realize the varying amounts that people might pay in and the varying number of years during which they might contribute, and so on. But that is not the meaning of contributory social insurance when you talk in state or national terms.
What we mean by contributory social insurance is that those who are working shall contribute to a fund out of which benefits are paid to those people who need them, whether because of ill health, unemployment or old

The Address-Mr. Knowles age. In return for those payments we who contribute now while we are earning would be entitled to benefits when we reached old age or when we found ourselves in some other situation where we needed them. In other words, it is quite different from setting up a fund into which money is put and out of which can be paid to each individual only what he has put in. A contributory scheme is in effect an arrangement whereby we plan our total production in any one year or in any one decade so that enough of that production can be used for the maintenance of those who need it because of unemployment, sickness or old age. In other words, social insurance is a charge on current production, and a contributory scheme is an arrangement to give effect to that principle.
A short while ago a very worth-while round table was held at the university of Toronto on this whole question of social security and a very interesting report was prepared by John S. Morgan, associate professor of social work at the University of Toronto. I should like to quote a few sentences from that report, as follows:
There was considerable argument as to who really pays the costs of social security, although all schemes have different apparent distributions of costs through employer's contributions, employee's contributions and state subsidies. It was recognized that, in the end result, all social security costs are a charge upon the productive capacity of the community. They may be hidden in the cost of repairing neglect, as for example in hospital costs, public assistance, prison and reformatory expenses and mental health expenditures; or they may be openly met by preventive and insurance measures. So far Canada has, in large measure, shirked the problem and preferred to keep the real costs of having no integrated plan for social security hidden in a complex tangle of federal, provincial and municipal responsibilities for patching and repairing the neglect of her human resources. The Canadian people are beginning to awaken to the need for something more constructive and more positive in their approach to social welfare.
I submit that that language is very much to the point. However, I should like to offer another quotation in connection with this matter of over-all social security and this time my authority is none other than Winston Churchill, who had something to say about it on March 21, 1943. I intend to quote from one of Mr. Churchill's many broadcasts made during the war years.

I am referring to Mr. Churchill's "Onwards to Victory", and I quote from pages 53 and 54:
The time is now ripe for another great advance, and anyone can see what large savings there will be in the administration, once the whole process of insurance has become unified, compulsory, and national. Here is a real opportunity for what I

once called "bringing the magic of averages to the rescue of the millions." Therefore, you must rank me and my colleagues as strong partisans of national compulsory insurance for all classes for all purposes from the cradle to the grave.
Incidentally Mr. Beland Honderich of the Toronto Daily Star recently pointed out that the life insurance companies are fond of quoting that sentence of Mr. Churchill's as though it was an endorsation of private life insurance. But I ask hon. members to note that "bringing the magic of averages to the rescue of the millions" is done by national compulsory social insurance, according to Mr. Churchill.

speechtext:
If the minister will only do what was suggested a little earlier today and hold his patience for a minute, I will answer his question. There is one other quotation that I want to give before I make my concluding remarks:
Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and of his family, including food, clothing, housing and medical care and necessary social services, and the right to security in the event of unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood in circumstances beyond his control.
That is from article 25 of the universal declaration of human rights which was passed by the general assembly of the United Nations last December, and for which Canada voted. I submit that the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), when he expressed Canada's views on this declaration of rights, should be accepted. He said that we accept this document "in the hope that it will mark a milestone in humanity's upward march." I strongly urge the government of this country to consider the wishes and desires of the Canadian people by giving full implementation to that article of the world bill of rights.
As members are aware, I speak on this subject repeatedly. I have done so a good many times on the basis of human interest. As the war came to a close I pleaded for old age security as a part of the new order that had been promised to us. Two years ago I spoke of it in relation to plans in other countries. Last year I made my case on the basis of the growing problem as shown by figures from the bureau of statistics. This time I have tried to document my plea by giving figures as to the inadequacy of the plans now in effect, good and all as they are. Indeed, I am convinced that it is our most important social problem.

In conclusion I would urge the government to do two things. One of them can be done immediately. The other, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) realizes from the question he interjected, does take a bit of time, but a beginning can be made immediately. The thing that can be done without delay is to increase the old age pension at this session to $50 a month payable at age sixty-five. That can be done by parliament by amendment of the Old Age Pensions Act. There is no question about it; we are all for it; it is up to the government to bring in the legislation. The other thing that takes time is to get a contributory plan under way. I am fully aware of the fact that that involves consultation and co-operation with the provinces; but the point is, it has got to get started some time; and if this government will give the lead, I am sure the provinces will agree. I insist that now is the time for action on this all-important question of proper old age security.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in offering my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Brown) and the seconder (Mr. Demers) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I am not attempting to continue the time-honoured custom, but I believe that I express the opinion of everyone in the house when I say that both members acquitted themselves very creditably in their difficult task. The hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) dealt with the subjects of his discourse in a masterly way, and showed that he had made a deep study of them.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I regret to notice that the new member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Demers) who seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne is not in the house. I should be very happy if I had his eloquence and fluency to tell him with what pleasure I listened to his maiden speech in this house.
As regards those who did not understand him, because they do not know his language, they certainly cannot have failed, while listening to him, to admire the beauty and harmony of the delectable French language.
He does honour to his province, because he has, in delivering his speech, given irrefutable proof of the fact that true education includes more than a mere smattering of sciences, certain other elements being indispensable, especially a deep knowledge of sound philosophy.
Consequently, if there are still among his own compatriots some who question the efficiency of the Quebec educational institutions, I believe his speech fully refuted their view and I am quite confident that Quebec
The Address-Mr. C. T. Richard is in no danger of being surpassed by the other provinces.
(Text):
There have been some notable changes in the house since we last met, changes which are probably unprecedented in our political history, because at one session we are welcoming the new leaders of the two major political groups. Although the session has only begun, they have shown great qualities of leadership. Incidentally, they are both possessed of very good looks, and they grace the front benches so well that it would be unfortunate if any event should disturb them. There is always a danger in transplanting, especially if either of them should be a little sensitive to any rough handling.
To the former Prime Minister, the right hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Mackenzie King), I have not much to say, because so many eloquent voices have been raised in the house to extol his qualities of mind, and the great achievements of his career, that I could not add very much. He has the consolation that his fondest dreams have been fulfilled. During his tenure of office and his long public career, he has seen enacted those measures which have brought such help and assistance towards banishing poverty and suffering, and bringing security to those in privation. There is no doubt that there are thousands and thousands of aged people, widows and orphans, who will bless him in years to come for having taken them out of the category of forgotten people.
I choose as the theme of my remarks the economic situation of the maritime provinces. In doing so I want to assure the house that I do not blame any political party for our situation. But while not blaming anybody,
I will not spare any either. I do not believe that we can attribute our economic situation in the maritimes to any particular regime, to any fixed period since confederation, or to any act or measure during those years which brought about such a change that, from being the most prosperous provinces at confederation, we have become the weakest link in the chain. Let me warn the house also that when I speak of the economic situation in the maritimes I mean the conditions which existed during normal times, and to which we will have to return after the effect of the boom years of the war is over.
There may be some who will take the recital of our grievances with no more consideration than complaints from any other province, but I want to say to the house that our grievances are real. They are of just as much concern to the people of Canada as a whole as they are to the people of the maritime provinces. This situation was recognized

The Address-Mr. C. T. Richard last year by the three major political parties when, at their respective conventions, they passed resolutions dealing with the problems of the maritimes.
In support of my argument that it is the concern of the whole nation that a solution be found, and that the million people inhabiting the maritime provinces be given a fair hearing at the bar of public opinion, let me quote from a survey which was prepared last year by the Department of Trade and Commerce, the data of which speak for themselves. I find this very significant paragraph in the report:
That area, speaking of the maritime provinces, has been beset by a long history of adverse economic conditions, small scale and near subsidized industry, vulnerability of specialized industry in Nova Scotia, and relative lack of urbanization and of accumulated wealth.
This survey also points out these very disturbing facts: that the income per capita in the maritime provinces ranges from 68 to 74 per cent of the average national income in Canada; that the total production per capita in the maritime provinces in 1945 was $533, compared with a national average of $963, or a difference of almost one hundred per cent; and that the total production of the maritime provinces was five per cent of the total for Canada, though we possess ten per cent of the population. The survey continues to show the great disparity between income, wealth and production in the maritimes and the figures for the entire dominion. Therefore anyone studying these figures must come to the conclusion that the economic situation in the maritimes is alarming.
There are those in the two largest provinces of this dominion who, viewing the growth of this country, its emergence from a colony to a full-fledged nation, its mounting population and so on, think of the smaller provinces, including the maritime provinces, as fortunate indeed to be associated in this confederation so they may profit by the overflowing wealth of the two great provinces. But let me point out, Mr. Speaker, that the maritimes did not always depend on others. The position of the maritime provinces at the time of confederation was quite different from what it is today. No better proof of that can be found than in a comparison of the figures I have cited as to wealth, production and income with the figures available as at the time of confederation. Let me point out also that contrasts always have the effect of making each of the contrasted objects appear in its strongest light. No better judges of the true position of the maritimes at confederation can be found than the leading statesmen of that day, who are now called the fathers of confederation. The maritime provinces were


self-sufficient. They possessed natural ports open to world trade the year round. They were in a favourable position to trade with the American states; and if they were barred from that market, all other markets in the world that could be reached by our ships were open to them. This enviable position was recognized by the most ardent advocates of confederation. I have quoted from the survey on economic conditions in the maritimes. Let me give by way of contrast the situation that existed at the time of confederation, and I quote Galt, at page 63 of the debates on confederation:
Taking the census of 1861, this trade represents thirty-five dollars per head of the population.
He is speaking of the trade of Upper and Lower Canada.
The value of the import and export trade of New Brunswick, for the same year, is $16,729,680, amounting to sixty-six dollars per head of its population.
That is, it was almost one hundred per cent greater than that of the upper Canadian provinces.
The aggregate trade of Nova Scotia for the same period amounted to $18,622,359 . . . and in the case of Prince Edward Island the import and export trade amounted to $3,055,568 . . .
Thus it will be seen that at the time of confederation our trade was more than fifty per cent higher than the trade of Upper and Lower Canada. As far as the revenues of the maritime provinces at the time of confederation were concerned, let me again quote Galt at page 66 of the debates:
It will be observed that as regards these provinces their income and expenditure are such that they will enter the confederation with a financial position in no respect inferior to that of Canada.
By "Canada" he meant the upper provinces.
If an objection were made with respect to any province in regard to its financial position, it would be against Canada. The lower provinces have been and are now in a position to meet, from their taxation, all their expenses, and cannot be regarded as bringing any burden to the people of Canada.
We are in a much humbler position today, Mr. Speaker. Time and again since confederation we have been forced to come to the central government to plead for increased subsidies in order to maintain our services, which always have been below the standards of those in other provinces. Let me repeat that we will never solve the economic problems of the maritime provinces by increased subsidies. That is a palliative which relieves the tension for a certain length of time, but it is never a cure. Bear in mind that at that period of our history we in the maritimes were not torn by strife, disunity and discord. We had already reached a spirit of compromise and understanding. Our leaders at the meeting at Charlottetown already were formulating a maritime union. When repre-

sentatives of the upper provinces reached Charlottetown during those deliberations, they were welcome but uninvited guests. They came as onlookers, not as negotiators for a federal union. They found so much progress had been made among the mari-timers toward a maritime union that they decided if a federal union were to materialize they must act at once. It was then that offers were made for a federal union.
On the other hand, what was the position of the upper provinces at that time? They were torn by dissatisfaction and disagreement; and again I quote Gait during the debates on confederation:
The house must not forget that it will forever remove the great and crying evils and dissensions which have existed in Canada for the last ten years, and which have threatened to plunge the country into the most disastrous and lamentable state of discord and confusion.
That was the situation in the upper provinces. I want to quote again from the debates on confederation. I hope I am not tiring you, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to prove my case from the very sayings of the fathers of confederation. Here is another extract:
Because just so surely as this scheme is defeated-
The speaker was referring to confederation. -will be evolved the original proposition for a union of the maritime provinces, irrespective of Canada . . . They will form themselves into a power which, though not so strong as if united with Canada, will nevertheless be a powerful and considerable community, and it will then be too late for us to attempt to strengthen ourselves by this scheme.
These are not the words of a maritimer speaking to his people; they are the words of the great Sir John A. Macdonald, addressed not to the maritimers but to his own people. Those words were meant to apply to the people of the upper provinces, as the next quotation from Sir John A. Macdonald shows:
If we are not blind to our present position, we must see the hazardous situation in which all the great interests of Canada stand in respect to the United States. I am no alarmist. I do not believe in the prospect of immediate war. I believe that the common sense of the two nations will prevent a war; still we cannot trust to probabilities ....
Our trade is hampered-
That was because of the civil war and differences between England and the United States.
-by the passport system and at any moment we may be deprived of permission to carry our goods through United States channels-the bonded goods system may be done away with . . . Our merchants may be obliged to return to the old system of bringing in during the summer months the supplies for the whole year. Ourselves already threatened, our trade interrupted, our intercourse, political and commercial, destroyed, if we do not take warning now when we have the opportunity, and while one avenue is threatened to be closed, open another by taking advantage of the present arrangement and the desire of the lower provinces to draw closer the
The Address-Mr. C. T. Richard alliance between us, we may suffer commercial and political disadvantages it may take long for us to overcome.
This was the situation in the upper Canadian provinces. Without an outlet to the sea, their foreign trade was bottlenecked and depended on the whims of our neighbours to the south.
In the confederation debates Cartier gives a clear comprehension of this handicap when he says, and I quote him:
Twenty years ago our commerce for the year could be managed by communication with Great Britain in the summer months only. At present, however, this system was insufficient and for winter communication with the seaboard we were left to the caprice of our American neighbours through whose territory we must pass. Canada having two or three elements of national greatness, territory and population, wanted the maritime element, and as he said, the lower provinces had this element and the seaboard.
Therefore, these words are applicable only to the upper Canadian provinces. We in the maritime provinces possessed that seaboard and had the choice of the United States or the overseas market. The entrance of the maritime provinces into confederation assured the provinces of upper Canada of this maritime element, as Cartier calls it, and assured their future prosperity which was then so precarious.
I have quoted copiously from these debates on confederation to show the exact picture of the maritimes at the time of confederation. Some people may consider such a review inappropriate, since it is all water under the bridge. However, we have to have recourse to such a study if we want to understand the real purpose of confederation. Macdonald called it a treaty, and as such it must be regarded. The pact of confederation must be read in the light of the conditions and circumstances in existence at the time it was effected.
Now, we maritimers have knowledge of all these facts. It is therefore somewhat galling to be always treated as if we were the adopted provinces of the two greater provinces, and that we should therefore be grateful to these more prosperous provinces for the bountiful munificence which overflows their boundaries. To use a common expression, we are getting sick and tired of it. I have quoted from the surveys certain figures which show that our economic situation is due to a lack of accumulated wealth and the growth of any industrial centres. The fathers of confederation felt that confederation would bring an increase in our industrial centres. This was held out as an inducement to the maritime provinces to sacrifice their wonderful position and enter a pact of confederation about which they were somewhat doubtful.

The Address-Mr. C. T. Richard
Have the cities of our Canadian seaboard had such a growth? The answer is to be found in a consideration of the expansion of the United States cities along the United States seaboard. When we consider that our cities have the same geographical position and the same climate, and that only an imaginary line separates the two of us, and when we consider the way our cities have steadily fallen behind, it is hard to understand how progress has passed us by.
There is a great deal of history connected with this matter of accumulated wealth and the development of our industrial centres on the Atlantic seaboard. Some may say this situation has come about because of uncontrollable events and that, confederation or no confederation, we would be in the same situation.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at seven-thirty o'clock.
